GC.19.stem: Most cases arrive at the U.S. Supreme Court through which type of jurisdiction?

choices.text: Appellate jurisdiction, on appeal from a lower court
Original jurisdiction, as the first court to hear the case
Legislative jurisdiction, referred by Congress
Executive jurisdiction, assigned by the President

GC.19.reteach: Revisit Article III, Section 2 and the close reading; contrast original vs. appellate jurisdiction with the 'a case starts here vs. an appeal arrives here' distinction.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Original jurisdiction exists but is the exception, not how most cases arrive — right topic, wrong frequency.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses the judicial branch with the legislative role; Congress does not refer cases up as 'jurisdiction.'

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses judicial jurisdiction with an executive assignment; the President does not route cases to the Court.

GC.19.key_rationale: Article III routes most cases to the Court on appeal from lower courts — appellate jurisdiction.
GC.19.dok_rationale: Students must interpret how cases reach the Court, not merely recall a term.
GC.19.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning by distinguishing two forms of jurisdiction.

GC.20.stem: Under the Constitution's 'Advice and Consent' requirement, which body must approve a Supreme Court nominee before that person can take the bench?

choices.text: The House of Representatives
The Senate
The state legislatures
The current Supreme Court justices

GC.20.reteach: Re-read Article II, Section 2; map the two-step process — President nominates, Senate confirms — and label who controls each step.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses the Senate's confirmation role with the House; the House does not confirm justices.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that states approve federal appointments; confirmation is a federal Senate power.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that the Court fills its own seats; sitting justices play no formal role.

GC.20.key_rationale: Article II gives the Senate the power of Advice and Consent to confirm nominees.
GC.20.dok_rationale: Students recall a single constitutional fact about who confirms nominees.
GC.20.blooms_rationale: Students retrieve the confirming body from memory.

GC.21.stem: Marbury v. Madison (1803) is most significant because it established which power of the courts?

choices.text: The power to collect federal taxes
The power to declare war on other nations
Judicial review — the power to declare a law unconstitutional and void
The power to choose the President in a tie

GC.21.reteach: Re-read Marshall's holding ('a law repugnant to the constitution is void'); define judicial review and connect it to checks and balances from Unit 1.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Taxing is a legislative power, not a judicial one established by Marbury.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Declaring war is a power of Congress, not a court power from Marbury.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Choosing a President in a tie is a House role under the 12th Amendment, unrelated to Marbury.

GC.21.key_rationale: Marshall's opinion established judicial review — courts may void a law that conflicts with the Constitution.
GC.21.dok_rationale: Students explain the significance of a landmark case, not just name it.
GC.21.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning about what power the ruling created.

GC.22.stem: A judge who defers to the elected branches and interprets the Constitution narrowly by its 'original intent' is practicing —

choices.text: judicial review
judicial activism
incorporation
judicial restraint

GC.22.reteach: Build a Frayer for judicial restraint vs. activism; sort short case summaries into 'defers to elected branches' vs. 'sets new policy.'

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Judicial review is the power itself, not the philosophy of how boldly to use it.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Activism is the opposite approach — greater willingness to strike down laws or set policy.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to the states; it is unrelated to activism vs. restraint.

GC.22.key_rationale: Deferring to elected branches and reading for original intent defines judicial restraint.
GC.22.dok_rationale: Students classify a described approach against a concept, requiring interpretation.
GC.22.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning by matching behavior to the correct philosophy.

formA.stem: The Constitution gives federal judges their offices 'during good Behaviour' — effectively for life — mainly to —

choices.text: guarantee that they can never be removed for any reason
protect their independence from political pressure so they can rule on the law
allow the President to replace them at the start of each term
require them to also serve as members of Congress

formA.reteach: Re-read Article III on tenure and pay protection; explain how life tenure trades democratic control for independence, and note that removal is only by impeachment.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralizes tenure; judges can be removed by impeachment, so 'never for any reason' is false.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that terms reset with each President; life tenure prevents this.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses the branches; judges do not also sit in Congress.

formA.key_rationale: Life tenure insulates judges from politics so they can decide cases on the law.
formA.dok_rationale: Students interpret the purpose behind a constitutional design feature.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students explain why the framers chose life tenure.

formA.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how a person becomes a U.S. Supreme Court justice?

choices.text: The Senate nominates; the President confirms by executive order
The current justices choose a successor and the President signs off
The President nominates; the Senate Judiciary Committee holds hearings; the full Senate confirms by majority vote
The states nominate a candidate and the House confirms the choice

formA.reteach: Diagram the confirmation flow: nomination → Judiciary Committee hearing → full Senate majority vote; label the branch responsible at each stage.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Reverses the roles; the President nominates and the Senate confirms, not the reverse.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that the Court is self-perpetuating; justices do not pick successors.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses the confirming body; states do not nominate and the House does not confirm justices.

formA.key_rationale: The correct order is Presidential nomination, Judiciary Committee hearing, then full-Senate confirmation.
formA.dok_rationale: Students order the steps of a process and match each to the correct actor.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students summarize the multi-step appointment procedure.

formA.stem: A federal law directly conflicts with a clause of the U.S. Constitution. Based on the reasoning in Marbury v. Madison, how should a court resolve the conflict?

choices.text: Enforce the law, because Congress passed it and courts must defer to Congress
Ask the President to decide which one controls
Send the question to the state legislatures for a vote
Treat the law as void, because the Constitution is the supreme law

formA.reteach: Apply Marshall's logic step by step: the Constitution is supreme, a conflicting law is void, and courts 'say what the law is'; practice with a hypothetical statute.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts Marbury; a law repugnant to the Constitution cannot simply be enforced.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses the branches; courts, not the President, decide constitutionality.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that states resolve constitutional conflicts; that is the judiciary's role.

formA.key_rationale: Marbury holds that a law conflicting with the supreme Constitution is void.
formA.dok_rationale: Students apply a precedent's reasoning to a new hypothetical conflict.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students use the Marbury rule to reach a conclusion in an unfamiliar case.

formA.stem: A court strikes down a long-standing law, reading the Constitution as a 'living document' that must adapt to new circumstances. This approach is best described as —

choices.text: judicial activism
judicial restraint
original jurisdiction
the rule of four

formA.reteach: Play 'Activist or Restrained?': classify rulings by whether the Court set new policy (activism) or deferred to elected branches and original text (restraint).

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Restraint is the opposite; it defers to elected branches and original intent rather than striking laws down.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Original jurisdiction is about which court hears a case first, not a judicial philosophy.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: The rule of four is how the Court agrees to hear a case, not how boldly it rules.

formA.key_rationale: Reading the Constitution as a living document and striking down a law reflects judicial activism.
formA.dok_rationale: Students analyze a scenario's reasoning to classify the judicial philosophy at work.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students break down the judge's approach to identify activism.

formB.stem: What distinguishes the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction from its appellate jurisdiction?

choices.text: Original jurisdiction means the Court is reviewing a lower court's decision
Original jurisdiction applies only to cases that begin in state courts
The two terms describe exactly the same kind of case
Original jurisdiction means the case is heard first at that court, not on appeal

formB.reteach: Use a two-column chart: 'starts here' (original) vs. 'arrives on appeal' (appellate); tie back to Article III, Section 2.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Reverses the definitions; reviewing a lower court is appellate, not original, jurisdiction.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Original jurisdiction is not limited to state-court origins; it is about hearing a case first.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that the two are identical; they describe different roles.

formB.key_rationale: Original jurisdiction means the Court hears the case first, not on appeal.
formB.dok_rationale: Students distinguish two related concepts by their defining feature.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning by contrasting original and appellate jurisdiction.

formB.stem: A Supreme Court seat opens with two years left in a President's term. Given how long a justice can serve, why might both parties in the Senate treat this single confirmation as unusually important?

choices.text: Because the new justice could shape the Court's decisions for decades, long after this President leaves office
Because the justice must be re-confirmed by the Senate every year
Because the House of Representatives will overturn the choice if it disagrees
Because the President loses all other powers while a confirmation is pending

formB.reteach: Connect life tenure (GC.19) to high-stakes confirmations: a decades-long term means one appointment outlasts the President who made it.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that justices face annual re-confirmation; they serve during good behavior.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: The House has no role in confirming or overturning a justice.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that a President is stripped of powers during a confirmation.

formB.key_rationale: A justice's decades-long tenure means one confirmation shapes the law far beyond the President's term.
formB.dok_rationale: Students reason from the consequence of life tenure to explain the political stakes.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students analyze cause and effect linking tenure length to confirmation intensity.

formB.stem: Judicial review is best defined as the power of courts to —

choices.text: propose new laws for Congress to consider
declare a law or government action unconstitutional and therefore void
remove the President from office through impeachment
set the federal budget each year

formB.reteach: Re-state the definition of judicial review in students' own words and pair it with the source case, Marbury v. Madison (1803).

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Proposing laws is a legislative function, not judicial review.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Impeachment is a congressional power, not judicial review.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Setting the budget is a legislative power, not a court power.

formB.key_rationale: Judicial review is the courts' power to void laws that conflict with the Constitution.
formB.dok_rationale: Students recall the definition of a key term.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students retrieve the meaning of judicial review from memory.

formB.stem: Reading the Constitution as a 'living document' and being more willing to strike down laws or set new policy reflects which judicial approach?

choices.text: judicial restraint
original jurisdiction
judicial activism
appellate review

formB.reteach: Contrast the 'living document' (activism) and 'original intent' (restraint) lenses; have students label a ruling and defend the label with evidence.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Restraint is the opposite approach — deference and original intent.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Original jurisdiction concerns which court hears a case first, not a philosophy.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Appellate review is a process, not the activism-vs-restraint philosophy.

formB.key_rationale: The 'living document' view with willingness to strike down laws is judicial activism.
formB.dok_rationale: Students match a described approach to the correct concept.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning by identifying the activist philosophy.

_psychometric_summary.note: IRT 3PL parameters are pre-field-test design-time estimates, to be calibrated on field-test data.
